title: How Google decides who is first

blocks.text: SEO (search engine optimization) is everything that makes Google show your site higher when people search for what you offer. Google does three things: it crawls your pages (reads them), indexes them (stores what each page is about) and ranks them (orders them for every search). You can only rank if the first two work.
What Google weighs

items: Relevance: does the page answer exactly what was searched? The words in the title, the headings and the text, and whether the page matches the intent (someone who searches "best habit tracker app" wants to compare apps, not read a history of habit science).
Trust: do other sites link to you, mention you, review you? A new site with no links ranks slowly, even with great content.
Experience: does the page load fast on a phone, is it readable, does it work without errors?
Clicks: when your result is shown, do people choose it and stay? A better title alone can move you up.

blocks.text: What Seenlab does on this page

items.title: Audit
items.text: Reads your site the way Google and AI crawlers do and lists what blocks you, most important first.

items.title: Rankings
items.text: Measures where you are on Google for the words you care about, on its schedule (every morning on Pro, Mondays on Free), and who is above you.

items.title: Research
items.text: Finds the searches worth winning and writes the plan for the page that deserves to be first.

items.title: Lab
items.text: Uses your Search Console data to find the fastest wins — pages that are seen but not clicked, queries almost on page 1 — and measures every change you make.

items.title: Plan
items.text: On its schedule picks the few actions with the biggest effect and writes the draft for each.

blocks.text: SEO is slow in the first weeks and then compounds. Do one thing from the plan every day and check the lab once a week — that routine beats a big rewrite once a year.

After the day’s measurements (every morning on Pro, Mondays on Free), Seenlab looks at every signal it has — Search Console, the audit, your Google positions, the AI answers — and turns each problem or opportunity into a possible action. Each one gets an estimated impact, and the strongest few make the plan.

items.label: Impact
items.text: For Search Console actions it is the extra clicks a month if the fix works (for example, a page on position 3 with a 1% CTR could get 11%). For other actions it is a relative score: a lost AI mention or a site-wide error scores high, a single weak internal link low.

items.label: Draft
items.text: The text to use: a new title and description, the email to an author, the corrected FAQ answer, the sentence and link to add. Copy it, adjust it to your voice and publish.

items.title: Open the first action
items.text: Read why it matters and the steps. The "Open" link takes you to the tab with all the details.

items.title: Use the draft
items.text: Edit it if needed and publish it on your site, send it, or paste it where the steps say.

items.title: Log it
items.text: For a page change, add an experiment in the Lab tab (the page and what changed) so Seenlab can show the effect.

blocks.text: "Refresh plan" writes a new plan now. It is also made automatically on the plan’s schedule, so you usually just open it.

The audit crawls up to 60 pages of your site like Google’s and the AI assistants’ crawlers do — without running JavaScript — and checks each page. It runs every Monday and whenever you press "Run again".

items.label: Score (0–100)
items.text: Starts at 100 and loses points for every issue per page: errors cost the most, notices the least. Above 80 is healthy; under 60 means something blocks Google.

items.label: Error
items.text: Blocks indexing or ranking: pages that return an error, pages that are empty without JavaScript, broken links, pages marked noindex by mistake.

items.label: Warning
items.text: Costs rankings or clicks: missing or duplicate titles, missing descriptions, no H1, slow pages.

items.label: Notice
items.text: Worth fixing when you have time: images without alt text, very short pages, missing social preview.

blocks.text: Open an issue to see which pages have it and how to fix it. Under the score you see the trend over the last audits and what was fixed or appeared since the previous one.

If your site shows its content only after JavaScript runs, most AI crawlers and part of Google see an empty page. The audit flags these pages as "Empty without JavaScript" — fix them first (server-side rendering or prerendering).

Internal links are links from one of your pages to another. Google follows them to find pages and to understand which ones matter. A page that no other page links to (an orphan) is found late or never, and it rarely ranks.

From the last crawl, Seenlab lists orphan pages and pages with a single link, and for each one the pages that talk about the same thing — the natural places to link from — with a suggested link text (anchor).

items.title: Open the suggested page
items.text: Find the paragraph where the topic is mentioned.

items.title: Add the link
items.text: Use the suggested anchor or a natural phrase that describes the target page. "Click here" tells Google nothing.

items.title: Two or three links per important page
items.text: Link each important page from at least two related pages and from a menu or hub page.

blocks.text: The anchor text is a small ranking signal for the target page: "habit tracker app" helps the app page more than "our product".

Add the searches you want to be first for. On its schedule (every morning on Pro, Mondays on Free) Seenlab reads Google’s results for each one, in the country you picked, and records your position, the page that ranks and the results above you.

items.label: Position
items.text: Your place among the organic results (ads excluded). "Outside top 20" means Seenlab read 20 results and you were not among them.

items.label: Trend
items.text: The last 30 days. Positions move a little every day; look at the direction over a week.

items.label: AI Overview
items.text: Whether Google shows an AI summary above the results for this search, and whether it cites your site. When it does not cite you, the AIO page shows how to get there.

items.label: Who outranks you
items.text: The sites that appear in the top 10 of your searches most often, and how many times they are above you. These are your real search competitors — often not the ones you think.

blocks.text: Where the numbers come from: with DataForSEO set up, Seenlab reads the real Google results (competitors and AI Overviews included). Without it, positions come from your Search Console — your own average position, without competitors.
Track 5–10 searches that bring customers, not the biggest words in your field. "Habit tracker app with widget" converts better than "app" and is winnable.

For a business with a place — a salon, a restaurant, a clinic — the map results are often worth more than the normal results. Seenlab searches "service + city" on Google Maps and shows your place and the businesses above you, with their ratings and number of reviews.
What decides the map order

items: Relevance: the category and services on your Google Business Profile match the search.
Distance: how close you are to the person searching (you cannot change it, which is why the city is part of the search).
Prominence: number and freshness of reviews, rating, photos, mentions and links around the web.

items.title: Claim and complete the profile
items.text: On business.google.com: the exact name, main category plus 2–3 extra ones, address, hours, phone, website, services with prices.

items.title: Photos
items.text: At least 10 real photos (outside, inside, work, team). Add new ones every month.

items.title: Reviews
items.text: Ask every happy customer, with a direct link. Answer every review, the bad ones calmly and quickly.

items.title: The same name everywhere
items.text: Name, address and phone written identically on your site, the profile and directories.

blocks.text: Enter your business name exactly as it appears on Google Maps, so Seenlab recognizes you in the results.
Type a topic and Seenlab lists what people search around it. With DataForSEO you also get the numbers; without it the ideas come from Google autocomplete (real searches, but without volumes).

items.label: Searches a month
items.text: How many times a month the search is made in that country. Rounded by Google.

items.label: Difficulty (0–100)
items.text: How hard it is to reach the top 10, from the strength of the sites there. Under 30 is realistic for a young site.

items.label: CPC
items.text: What advertisers pay per click. A high CPC means the search brings buyers.

items.label: Your site
items.text: Your impressions and position for that search from Search Console — if you already show up, it is the easiest win.

blocks.text: The best words are specific, have buying intent and moderate difficulty: "habit tracker app with reminders" rather than "habits". "Track" adds it to Rankings; "Content plan" writes the page for it.

For one search, Seenlab reads the pages that are on top (their titles, headings and length) and your page, and writes what your page is missing and a plan for the page that deserves to be first: the intent, the structure (H2 sections and what each says), a title, a meta description, FAQ questions, an opening paragraph and where to link from.

items.title: Start from the intent
items.text: If the top pages are comparisons and yours is a product page, you need a comparison, not more keywords.

items.title: Cover the missing topics
items.text: The red chips are what the top pages cover and yours does not. Add a section for each that makes sense.

items.title: Publish and link
items.text: Use the title and description, add the FAQ, link the page from 2–3 related pages.

items.title: Log the change
items.text: Add an experiment in the Lab tab to see the effect in 2–3 weeks.

blocks.text: Google Search Console is Google’s free tool that shows how your site does in search: for which searches it was shown (impressions), how often people clicked (clicks, CTR) and at which average position. It is the most reliable data there is, because it comes from Google.

items.title: Verify your site
items.text: On search.google.com/search-console add your domain and verify it (usually a DNS record at your domain provider).

items.title: Connect it in Seenlab
items.text: In the Search Console tab press Connect and choose the property. Access is read-only.

items.title: Wait for the first data
items.text: Seenlab imports the last 90 days and then syncs every day. Google’s data is 2–3 days behind.

blocks.text: The Lab, the demand prompts on the AIO page and a big part of the morning plan run on Search Console data. It is the single most valuable thing to connect.

CTR (click-through rate) is the share of people who saw your result and clicked it. Every position has a typical CTR; when yours is far below it, the title and description are the problem — not the ranking. It is the fastest fix in SEO: no new content, only a better snippet.

Seenlab lists pages on page 1 with a CTR under 60% of the typical value and shows the extra clicks a month if they reached it. "New titles" writes three titles and two descriptions for the searches that bring the page.

items: Put the searched words at the start of the title.
Promise a concrete result or number ("in 2 minutes", "free for 14 days").
Match the intent: a comparison search wants "vs", a how-to search wants "how to".
Keep the title under 60 characters and the description under 155, or Google cuts them.

blocks.text: "Use this one" logs an experiment for the page, so in two weeks you see whether the CTR really went up.

Searches where you are on positions 8–20 already have Google’s trust: a small push moves them to the top five, where the clicks are. Seenlab lists them with the clicks a month you would get on position 3.

items.title: Check the page
items.text: Does it answer that exact search? If the query is not in the title and a heading, add it.

items.title: Add what is missing
items.text: "Content plan" shows what the top pages cover that yours does not.

items.title: Link to it
items.text: Two or three internal links from related pages, with the search phrase as the anchor.

blocks.text: Start with the searches that have the most impressions — the same effort brings the most clicks.

Pages whose clicks in the last 28 days fell by 30% or more compared with the 28 days before. Usual reasons: the content got old (prices, years, screenshots), a competitor published something better, or Google now answers the question itself.

items.title: Compare the position
items.text: If the position dropped, the page lost to others — refresh the content. If the position is the same and clicks fell, the snippet or the search results changed — refresh the title.

items.title: Refresh
items.text: Update facts and the year, add what is new, improve the title. "Refresh" writes new titles for the page.

blocks.text: Every change to a page is an experiment. Log it the day it goes live (the page and what you changed) and Seenlab compares the page’s clicks per day, CTR and position in the 14 days before with the 14 days after, skipping the first 3 days while Google re-reads the page.

items: Change one thing at a time on a page, or you will not know what worked.
Wait for "result ready" (at least 5 measured days after); earlier numbers are noise.
Clicks per day can move with the season; CTR and position show the effect of a title better.

blocks.text: Keep what worked, roll back what did not, and use the winner’s pattern on similar pages.
AI assistants read your site with their own crawlers. If they cannot read it, they cannot recommend it. The AI readiness tab checks three things.

items.label: Bots
items.text: Your robots.txt decides which crawlers may read the site. You may block training bots (GPTBot, CCBot, Google-Extended), but keep the search bots (OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, PerplexityBot, Claude-SearchBot, Googlebot, Bingbot) allowed, or you disappear from answers.

items.label: llms.txt
items.text: A short markdown map of the site for AI assistants: what the product is and which pages matter. Seenlab drafts it; upload it to the root of your site.

items.label: Content without JavaScript
items.text: Most AI crawlers do not run JavaScript. A page that is empty without it is empty for them.

blocks.text: Schema markup (next chapter) and IndexNow (the one after) also belong here: both help assistants find and describe you correctly.

Schema is a small block of structured data (JSON-LD) in the page that tells Google and AI assistants exactly what the page is: a software product with a price, a business with an address and hours, a list of questions with answers. Google uses it for rich results; assistants use it to describe you correctly.

items.title: Generate
items.text: "Write schema" creates the blocks from your site and your product facts. It never invents prices or reviews.

items.title: Paste
items.text: Put each block in the <head> of the page it says (usually the home page and the pricing or FAQ page).

items.title: Test
items.text: Check it with Google’s Rich Results Test (search.google.com/test/rich-results).

blocks.text: Only mark up what is visible on the page. Schema with fake reviews or prices that are not on the page can get the site penalized.

ChatGPT search and Microsoft Copilot find pages through Bing’s index. If Bing does not know your pages, those assistants cannot cite them. IndexNow is a free standard that tells Bing (and Yandex, Seznam, Naver) the moment a page is new or changed, instead of waiting for a crawl.

items.title: Upload the key file
items.text: Seenlab gives you a key. Create a text file named <key>.txt whose only content is the key, and put it at the root of your site (the address is shown).

items.title: Check
items.text: "Check" confirms the file is there.

items.title: Send the pages
items.text: "Send pages" submits the pages from the last crawl. Do it again after you publish or change something important.

blocks.text: Also add your site to Bing Webmaster Tools (bing.com/webmasters) — it can import everything from Google Search Console in one click.
